groups.title: Input Validation
groups.question: Explain how you validate untrusted input at the edge of a Node.js API.

followUps.Zod Schema Validation: Why is a schema library like Zod better than hand-written if checks for request validation?
followUps.Zod + TypeScript Type Inference: What problem does z.infer solve compared with writing a separate interface?

evidence.text: A schema describes the expected shape, types and limits in one place instead of scattered if checks.
It checks everything consistently, including nested fields, and returns clear errors listing what's wrong.
Parsing returns clean typed data or rejects the request, so handlers only see valid input.

notEnough: Only saying use Zod to validate without explaining why it beats hand-written checks.

evidence.text: z.infer derives a TypeScript type from the schema.
The runtime check and the static type then come from one definition and can't drift apart, unlike a separate interface.

notEnough: Only saying z.infer creates a type without explaining the drift problem.

misconceptions.text: Says TypeScript types alone validate request data at runtime.

groups.title: Error Handling Architecture
groups.question: Walk through how errors flow from deep in your code to a clean HTTP response.

followUps.Centralized Error Handler: What problems show up when each route formats its own errors?
followUps.Custom Error Classes: How do custom error classes help a global error handler pick the right status code?

evidence.text: One global error handler turns every thrown or passed error into the HTTP response.
When each route formats its own errors, responses are inconsistent, internals like stack traces can leak, and some errors are missed.

notEnough: Only saying use a global error handler without explaining what goes wrong without one.

evidence.text: Custom error classes, like NotFoundError or ValidationError, extend Error and carry a status code or type.
The global handler checks the class or its status to choose the response code and message.
Errors that aren't known classes become a generic 500 without exposing details.

notEnough: Only saying create custom errors without explaining how the handler uses them.

groups.title: Layered Architecture
groups.question: Explain how you split a Node.js backend into layers and why.

followUps.Route → Service → Repository Pattern: What does a repository layer let you do in tests that you could not do with queries in route handlers?
followUps.Dependency Injection Patterns: How does dependency injection make a payment service easier to test?

evidence.text: Routes handle HTTP, services hold business logic, and repositories handle data access.
With queries behind a repository, tests can replace it with a fake and test the service logic without a database.

notEnough: Only listing the layers without explaining the benefit for tests.

evidence.text: Dependency injection means a service receives its dependencies, like a payment client, instead of creating or importing them itself.
In a test you pass a fake payment client, so you can check success and failure without charging real money.

notEnough: Only defining dependency injection without showing how it helps testing.

groups.title: Configuration Management
groups.question: Explain how you manage configuration and logging for a production Node.js service.

followUps.Validated Config with env-schema: Why is failing at startup better than failing on the first request when config is wrong?
followUps.Structured Logging with Pino: Why are structured JSON logs more useful in production than console.log strings?

evidence.text: Config is checked against a schema at startup: required values exist and have the right types.
A wrong config then stops the service before it serves traffic, with a clear error, instead of failing on a real user's request.

notEnough: Only saying validate config without explaining why at startup.

evidence.text: Structured logs are JSON objects with fields like level, time, request ID and message.
Log tools can filter and search them by field, which plain console.log strings don't allow.
Pino writes them with very little overhead, which matters in a busy service.

notEnough: Only saying use Pino without explaining why structured logs help.
